beats.scene: COLD OPEN — The Night the Water Left
beats.summary: Serene, almost lullaby-paced legend: moonlit ocean, then the tide going out and simply never stopping — a century compressed into dissolves as a harbor dries, ships settle into salt, a town climbs its cliff. Narration legend (the episode's only narration): the ocean withdrew in one night; nobody knows where it went; by old law, every light, every night. We end present-day on Saltwick Light's beam sweeping a sea of air — and where the beam is NOT, the darkness below reads a shade too deep, like depth. No monster. Just wrongness withheld.

The beam swings into camera — whiteout — and the title 'SALTGLASS: Six Minutes' resolves as letters grown in salt crystal on black. Audio: wind, and one small bell, very far away, rung once. (First plant of the bell motif; it will mean 'someone is crossing' by episode's end.)

beats.scene: LOW TIDE OF A HUNDRED YEARS — warm morning
beats.summary: Golden dawn on the seabed: Espen scavenging among stone kelp and a whale ribcage, prying loose a shard of saltglass, breath fogging, utterly at home in the dead sea. Orla summons him up the cliff stair by ringing the lighthouse's brass signal bell — their private language. Breakfast in the lamp room: dry jokes, her salt-stiff hands fumble the kettle and she covers it with humor; he doesn't clock it, we do. Turn: he wants to sell his jar of 'pretty junk' for a bicycle wheel; she rules lamp oil comes first, again, and he pockets the jar in silent protest.

beats.scene: THE MERCHANT — the town doesn't believe either
beats.summary: Espen hauls the oil can into a cliff-town of drying laundry and boredom. Merchant Bren short-measures the oil and needles him: a hundred years, not one ship, your gran burns money for ghosts — and Espen, for the first time out loud, agrees. Turn: he keeps the skimmed change instead of arguing, a small betrayal of the lamp he'll pay for tonight. On the walk home Bren squints across the strait — 'Funny. Can't see Farholm's light lately. Haze, probably' — and nobody, including the audience, is asked to worry about it yet.

Dusk ritual, taught in close-ups of hands: trim the wick, warm the oil, strike, count — Orla's litany, 'never let full dark touch the floor of the sea.' Espen parrots it while spinning his saltglass jar, and she does something out of character: grips his wrist hard and says the lamp can be dark six minutes, no more, then stops herself before saying what happens at seven. Turn: the first crack in the warm surface — she's not eccentric, she's afraid. Plants paid later: the counting, and the match tin on the sill with eight matches left ('buy more tomorrow').

beats.scene: STORM SUPPER — the last warm minute
beats.summary: Peak warmth, deliberately held: supper in the lamp room while the storm walls up over the strait like something beautiful, lantern light on two faces, Orla lands a joke and Espen actually laughs. She takes a folded paper of powder with her tea when his back is turned — the illness, shown once, never spoken. She sends him to bed; last image of the old world is her silhouette small against the burning lamp. The episode's front ten minutes end here, on comfort.

Espen wakes in black to the signal bell ringing irregular, dragged — their private language, broken. He finds the stair door blown open, rain coming up the spiral, and Orla collapsed on the landing, one hand still tangled in the bell rope. Above them, the true horror delivered in a single tilt-up: the lamp room is dark — the gust that took her took the flame. Turn: she can't stand, he can't lift her, and her only line sends a twelve-year-old past his dying grandmother: 'The light. Go.'

beats.scene: SIX MINUTES — the sea comes back
beats.setpiece: BIGGEST SETPIECE — near-real-time, the six dark minutes played almost at length
beats.summary: Near-real-time and nearly wordless: spilled oil slicks the striker, match one dies in the draft, match two snaps at the head, and Espen counts aloud the way she taught him because it's all he has. In his pocket the saltglass jar wakes — a faint blue that keeps brightening — and outside the gallery glass the storm changes physics: rain stops falling and starts streaming sideways, like current, and pressure-creaks run through the tower like a hull ten fathoms down. The score drops out entirely as fin-lights rise past the windows and an eye the size of the supper table pauses level with the boy; he uses the jar's glow to find the dropped tin and shields the last match inside Orla's hanging coat. Turn: the wick catches on match eight — light hits the 'water' like dry land slamming back into existence, the sea recoils, and one long whale-deep note sinks away below the cliff. Espen believes.

The rest of the night is compressed exactly as hard as the dark was stretched: dissolves of Espen feeding the wick, dragging Orla to the daybed by inches, sitting with his back against the lamp column with the now-dark jar beside the flame like a spent gauge. He performs the ritual full and correct, lips moving through her litany. Turn: the chore has become a vigil; the boy who skimmed oil money is guarding a shoreline.

Storm gone; the seabed steams gold and looks, for one cruel beat, almost like water again. Orla wakes on the daybed and neither of them narrates the night — she just sees seven burnt matches lined up on the sill and the eighth's empty slot, and her face does the arithmetic. His hand is shaking as he pours her tea; her stiff hand steadies it. Turn, all subtext: he says 'I'll buy more matches,' and she answers 'Buy two tins' — the apprenticeship is real now, and so is her time running out.

Sound first: dozens of small bells rising from the seabed, paying off the motif — in a world where the dark listens, a crosser announces himself like a lit lamp made of noise. The Bellfarer crests the cliff stair, wide hat, coat sewn with bells, license papers held up before his face is even visible. His news lands flat and terrible in the morning light: Farholm Light, across the strait, went dark three weeks ago — and no one has come off that cliff since. He looks past Orla to the boy standing in front of the still-burning lamp: 'Who keeps this one?' Espen, first time in his life: 'I do.'

Tease: full daylight across the strait — Farholm's tower with its lamp-room glass broken outward, and in the long shadow pooled at its base, something is still swimming. In shadow. In daylight. End card: the title re-crystallizes in salt; one far bell.

hook_ending: The hook is delivered in daylight, which is the point: bells announce the Bellfarer, the first outsider of the series, who reports that Farholm Light across the strait has been dark for three weeks with no survivors seen — then asks 'Who keeps this one?' and Espen claims the lamp out loud for the first time. The tease weaponizes the episode's one rule (dark = water) by showing it breaking: at Farholm, something swims in a pool of SHADOW at noon. Safety was never 'daytime.' It was light — and light can be lost.
why_it_works: The structure is a tide chart: ten unbroken minutes of warm, tactile, ordinary life (breakfast, short-measured oil, a lesson, a joke over supper) so the audience relaxes into the same disbelief Espen holds — the lamp is a museum piece, the rules are superstition. Every warm beat secretly loads a gun (eight matches, the six-minute rule, the bell language, the jar, the powder in the tea, 'can't see Farholm lately'), so the back half fires nothing it didn't plant in comfort. Then the disaster is compressed into one hinge scene and the six dark minutes are played nearly real-time — a 4-minute setpiece for a 6-minute event — inverting the episode's time signature so dark feels longer than the whole day that preceded it. This pacing suits the renderer perfectly: the horror is composition and sound (a glowing jar, an eye at the glass, score dropping to hull-creaks, silence between subtitle events), not choreography or facial acting, and the subtitle budget stays low because the front half is domestic small-talk and the back half is almost mute. Second viewing rewards: Orla's fumbled kettle, the wrongly-deep dark under the cold-open beam, Bren's 'haze, probably,' and the bell motif that starts as a grandmother's dinner call and ends as the only sound that keeps a man alive on the seabed.
risks: Three real risks. (1) The front-loaded warmth can go slack if the ordinary beats lack micro-tension — each must still turn (the skimmed change, the wrist-grip, the hidden powder) or minutes 2-10 feel like setup. (2) The near-real-time setpiece bets everything on the engine's dark-scene rendering and sound design; if the blacks crush or the silence isn't mixed with discipline, 'eternal' becomes 'slow.' (3) Creature exposure: one clear eye is the ceiling — any more of the Undertow and dread collapses into monster-of-the-week; the fix is to light Espen and the glass, never the thing itself.
